subtopic_detail: Leakage only on coughing and running eight months after a second vaginal birth with a normal bladder diary and no urgency
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33 year old woman eight months after the vaginal birth of her second child. She leaks a small amount of urine when she coughs, sneezes or runs after her toddler, and has stopped going to her exercise class because of it.

She never leaks on the way to the toilet and does not get a sudden overwhelming need to go. She empties her bladder five times a day and does not wake at night for it. Her bladder diary shows a normal fluid intake of 1.8 litres and voided volumes between 250 and 400 mL. She has completed her family and is not breastfeeding. Examination shows a well healed perineum and she can hold a voluntary pelvic floor contraction for three seconds.

data_table.Examination: Well healed second degree perineal repair, no vaginal wall descent on Valsalva, voluntary pelvic floor contraction palpable but weak and held for 3 seconds, leakage of a small volume of urine observed on cough with a comfortably full bladder, post void residual volume 25 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine negative on culture, urine dipstick negative for blood nitrites and glucose

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for a supervised pelvic floor muscle training programme of at least three months
options.rationale: Leakage confined to effort with no urgency and a normal diary defines the effort related pattern, and supervised training with a continence physiotherapist cures or substantially improves the majority and is recommended before any drug or operation. Supervision matters because unsupervised leaflets produce markedly poorer results. (Source: Continence Foundation of Australia: Urinary incontinence in women)
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Urinary incontinence in women

options.text: Refer to a urogynaecologist for a midurethral sling on the next available elective list
options.rationale: Surgery is considered only after an adequate supervised conservative programme has failed, and in Australia sling procedures now carry a formal informed consent and audit pathway. Offering it first skips the treatment that would resolve most cases without a permanent implant. (Source: RANZCOG: Midurethral slings)

options.text: Start an antimuscarinic and arrange a bladder training programme with fluid advice
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy and bladder retraining treat urgency with frequency and urgency leakage, and the near pair is that both patterns leak urine but only one is preceded by an overwhelming need to void. She never leaks on the way to the toilet. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology)

options.text: Arrange urodynamic studies before committing her to any particular treatment pathway
options.rationale: Urodynamics is reserved for mixed or unclear symptoms, previous continence surgery, voiding difficulty or a discordant history, since it does not improve outcomes in straightforward effort related leakage. Her diary, examination and cough test are all concordant. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen and review her symptoms again in three months
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen helps leakage associated with urogenital atrophy after menopause, which produces pale thin tissue and often urgency as well. She is 33 with well oestrogenised tissue and no atrophy to treat. (Source: Australian Menopause Society: Vaginal oestrogen)

explanation.summary: Urinary leakage affects about one in three Australian women at some point and the first task is to separate effort related leakage from urgency leakage, because the treatments diverge completely. Effort related leakage happens instantaneously with a rise in abdominal pressure, involves small volumes, and is not preceded by a warning sensation, while urgency leakage follows a sudden compelling need and often involves larger volumes and night waking. A bladder diary over three days, a urine culture to exclude infection, a post void residual and a cough test with a comfortably full bladder answer most questions without specialised testing. Supervised pelvic floor training for at least three months is first line for effort related leakage, with continence pessaries or surgery considered after that, and duloxetine occupying a small niche for women who decline both.
key_points: Leakage without a preceding urge indicates an effort related mechanism
A three day bladder diary and a post void residual guide most decisions
Supervised training outperforms written instructions given alone
Urodynamics is for discordant, mixed or previously operated cases
Surgery follows an adequate conservative trial, not the other way around
explanation.pearls: A minimum of three months of supervised training with at least eight contractions three times daily is the benchmark before declaring conservative therapy to have failed, and a woman who cannot produce a palpable voluntary contraction at all should be taught with biofeedback rather than sent away with a handout.

subtopic_detail: Three second trimester losses at 16 to 19 weeks with painless cervical dilatation twice and a normal antiphospholipid and karyotype screen
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32 year old woman in the recurrent loss clinic. She has had three pregnancies, lost at 16, 18 and 19 weeks, and on two of those occasions the membranes were found bulging through an open cervix when she presented with pressure but no contractions and no bleeding.

She has never had a term birth. She has had no cervical surgery and no procedures on the uterus. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies were negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin are normal, and parental karyotypes are normal. A transvaginal ultrasound today reports a heart shaped uterine cavity with a broad midline indentation and a smooth flat external fundal contour.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, cervix closed and 3 cm long on speculum with no scarring, uterus anteverted and normal size, adnexae non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent, parental karyotypes normal, transvaginal ultrasound showing a midline cavity indentation of 12 mm with an external fundal contour that is flat

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic resection of the midline tissue on the next available theatre list
options.rationale: Resection is the treatment once a septum is confirmed, but operating on a fused double horned uterus on the basis of the cavity shape alone risks entering the myometrium and perforating. The external contour is what separates the two and it has not yet been measured properly. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Arrange three dimensional ultrasound to define the cavity and fundal contour precisely
options.rationale: A deep midline indentation with a flat external contour suggests a residual septum rather than a fused double horned uterus, and the two are managed completely differently, so the contour must be measured before anyone operates. Coronal three dimensional imaging gives that measurement without an anaesthetic and is the recommended first line test. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Arrange elective cervical cerclage at 12 weeks in her next pregnancy without imaging
options.rationale: A history based suture is a genuine option for painless mid trimester dilatation, and it may still be offered later, but committing to it while an untreated structural cause is on the scan attributes the losses to the cervix alone. The near pair is that both conditions produce painless second trimester loss and they can coexist. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency)

options.text: Start low dose aspirin with prophylactic low molecular weight heparin in the next pregnancy
options.rationale: Combined aspirin and heparin is the treatment for antiphospholipid syndrome, which requires a persistently positive antibody on two occasions twelve weeks apart. Both sets of her antibodies were negative, so this treats a disease she does not have. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Start vaginal progesterone from 16 weeks in the next pregnancy and monitor her cervix
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth in women with a short cervix measured in the current pregnancy, which is a surveillance based decision made after 16 weeks. It is not a substitute for defining a uterine anomaly before she conceives. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Recurrent pregnancy loss is investigated for antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid and glucose control, parental chromosomes and uterine structure, and in a woman with mid trimester losses the uterine cavity carries more weight than it does with early losses. The critical structural distinction is between a septate uterus, where a fibrous midline partition sits inside a single fused muscular body with a normal external contour, and a bicornuate uterus, where the external fundus is indented because the two horns never fused. Only the first is amenable to hysteroscopic resection, which improves live birth rates, whereas resecting the midline of a bicornuate uterus risks perforation and does not help. Three dimensional ultrasound in the coronal plane has largely replaced laparoscopy with hysteroscopy as the way to measure the external contour and the depth of the indentation.
key_points: Mid trimester painless loss raises both cervical and structural causes
The external fundal contour separates a septate from a bicornuate uterus
Only a septum is treated by hysteroscopic resection
Three dimensional coronal imaging replaces laparoscopy for the contour
Antiphospholipid treatment requires persistently positive antibodies
explanation.pearls: An external fundal indentation deeper than 10 mm below the interostial line indicates a bicornuate uterus rather than a septum, and that single measurement decides whether hysteroscopic resection is safe or contraindicated.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Recurrent pregnancy loss

subtopic_detail: Sixteen year old with no menstruation, full breast development, sparse pubic hair and a short blind ending vagina with bilateral groin swellings
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 16 year old who has never menstruated. Her breasts developed at 12 and she has grown to 176 cm, taller than both parents.

She has almost no pubic or axillary hair, which she says has never bothered her. She has never had cyclical abdominal pain of any kind. She has a firm mobile swelling in each groin that her mother assumed were hernias. On examination the external genitalia are female and the vagina is 4 cm long and ends blindly. A pelvic ultrasound performed this morning reports no uterus and no ovaries, with soft tissue structures in both inguinal canals.

data_table.Examination: Height 176 cm, Tanner stage 5 breast development, Tanner stage 1 to 2 pubic and axillary hair, normal female external genitalia, vagina 4 cm long ending blindly with no cervix visible, firm mobile 3 cm swelling in each inguinal canal, no acne or clitoromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound with no uterus and no ovaries identified and soft tissue structures in both inguinal canals, testosterone 18 nanomoles per litre (female range 0.5-2.6), luteinising hormone 14 international units per litre, follicle stimulating hormone 5 international units per litre, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and both inguinal canals with contrast
options.rationale: Imaging maps the gonads and any rudimentary structures, and it will be needed when planning gonadectomy, but it cannot say which chromosomes are present. Ultrasound has already shown the essential anatomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

options.text: Measurement of serum anti Mullerian hormone with inhibin B on a morning sample
options.rationale: These markers reflect gonadal tissue activity and are elevated in this condition, which is supportive rather than diagnostic, since the same pattern occurs in other disorders of sex development. They do not identify the chromosomal complement. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Disorders of sex development)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Disorders of sex development

options.text: Karyotype analysis on a peripheral blood sample sent to a cytogenetics laboratory
options.rationale: Full breast development with absent pubic hair, a male range testosterone and an absent uterus indicate a 46 XY individual whose tissues cannot respond to androgen, with breast growth driven by aromatised oestrogen. The karyotype distinguishes this from absent uterine development in a 46 XX individual, which is the other cause of a blind vagina at this age. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Measurement of serum 17 hydroxyprogesterone with a short synacthen stimulation test
options.rationale: Adrenal enzyme testing is for virilisation of a 46 XX individual, which presents with excess rather than absent sexual hair and with ambiguous genitalia in infancy. Her pattern is the opposite, with absent hair and unvirilised external genitalia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy of the structures found in both inguinal canals
options.rationale: Histology of the gonads is obtained at the time of planned removal rather than as the diagnostic step, and an operation before the chromosomes are known risks removing tissue that is the source of her oestrogen. The near pair is that biopsy and karyotype both identify the gonadal type but only one is a blood test. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

explanation.summary: Absent menstruation with a blind ending vagina and no uterus on imaging has two principal explanations in adolescence, and the sexual hair pattern separates them at the bedside. A 46 XX individual with absent uterine and upper vaginal development has normal pubic and axillary hair, functioning ovaries, normal female testosterone and often associated renal or skeletal anomalies. A 46 XY individual whose androgen receptor does not function has sparse or absent sexual hair, a male range testosterone, gonads that may sit in the inguinal canals, and taller than average stature. Management in the second case includes disclosure handled by an experienced multidisciplinary team, oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy, vaginal dilators where the vagina is short, and a discussion of gonadal tumour risk that guides the timing of removal.
key_points: Absent pubic hair with full breast development suggests androgen insensitivity
A male range testosterone in a phenotypic female is the decisive laboratory clue
Karyotype separates the two main causes of a blind vagina with no uterus
Gonads in the inguinal canal in this setting are testes, not ovaries
Normal pubic hair with an absent uterus points to Mullerian agenesis instead
explanation.pearls: The malignant potential of intra-abdominal gonads in complete androgen insensitivity is low before puberty but rises with age, so current practice defers gonadectomy until after spontaneous pubertal breast development is complete rather than removing them in childhood.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Disorders of sex development

subtopic_detail: Four months of bloating and early satiety in a postmenopausal woman with a solid adnexal mass with papillary projections and ascites
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old woman who has felt bloated for four months and now fills up after a few mouthfuls. She has lost 4 kg without trying and has been to the toilet more often to pass urine.

She went through menopause at 51 and has had no vaginal bleeding. She was treated for irritable bowel symptoms for the last three months without improvement. Her mother died of ovarian cancer at 58 and a maternal aunt had breast cancer at 44. Abdominal examination finds shifting dullness and a firm mass arising from the pelvis. The ultrasound she had yesterday describes a 9 cm solid mass with papillary projections and internal blood flow, with free fluid in the abdomen.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended with shifting dullness, firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis reaching 5 cm above the symphysis, no hepatomegaly, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no vaginal bleeding on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound showing a 9 cm solid adnexal mass with papillary projections and internal vascularity plus moderate ascites, CA125 640 units per millilitre (less than 35), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), albumin 33 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly to a gynaecological oncology centre for staging and multidisciplinary care
options.rationale: A postmenopausal woman with a solid vascular adnexal mass, ascites and a markedly raised marker has a high risk of malignancy, and survival is better when primary surgery is performed by a subspecialist within a multidisciplinary service. That referral is made on the clinical and imaging picture rather than after further local tests. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer to the general gynaecology list for laparoscopic removal of the adnexal mass
options.rationale: Laparoscopic removal of a suspicious mass outside a specialist centre risks rupture and upstaging, and it leaves the woman without the full staging procedure she is likely to need. The near pair is that the same operation in a specialist unit forms part of a planned cytoreduction. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer to the interventional suite for diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis this week
options.rationale: Drainage relieves symptomatic distension and cytology can support the diagnosis, but neither changes the destination and a paracentesis performed first can delay the specialist referral. Symptom relief is arranged by the receiving unit as part of the plan. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy and gastroscopy to exclude a gastrointestinal primary tumour first
options.rationale: A gastrointestinal primary with ovarian deposits is worth considering when the masses are bilateral with a normal marker or when bowel symptoms dominate, and endoscopy is then arranged by the treating team. Making it the first step delays definitive referral by weeks. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer for genetic counselling and germline testing before any surgical decision is taken
options.rationale: Her family history does warrant germline testing and it is now offered to all women with this diagnosis, but it is arranged alongside treatment rather than before it. Waiting for a genetics appointment before referral costs time that affects outcome. (Source: eviQ: Ovarian cancer genetic testing)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer is diagnosed late in three quarters of Australian women because the early symptoms of bloating, early satiety, abdominal pain and urinary frequency are common and non-specific, and they are frequently attributed to irritable bowel syndrome. New onset of these symptoms in a woman over 50, particularly if persistent for more than a few weeks, should prompt pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound and a CA125. Features that raise concern on imaging are solid components, papillary projections, internal vascularity, bilaterality and ascites. Referral to a gynaecological oncology service confers a measurable survival benefit through complete staging and optimal cytoreduction, and germline testing is now offered to every woman with high grade serous disease because it guides both her treatment and her relatives' risk.
key_points: Bloating and early satiety in a woman over 50 warrant pelvic imaging
Irritable bowel syndrome rarely presents for the first time after 50
Solid components, papillary projections and ascites raise malignancy risk
Subspecialist surgery improves survival and completeness of staging
Germline testing is offered to all women with high grade serous disease
explanation.pearls: A new diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome made after the age of 50 should be treated as a diagnostic red flag rather than a label, because it is the single commonest misattribution recorded in the months before an ovarian cancer diagnosis.

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain with fever at 24 weeks where the appendix is not visualised on ultrasound and the white cell count sits in the physiological pregnancy range
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy with 18 hours of abdominal pain. It began around her navel and has settled into the right side of her abdomen above the level of her navel, and she has vomited twice and cannot face food.

She has no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms and no vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid. Foetal movements are normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring. She is tender in the right abdomen with voluntary guarding but no rebound. Her urine dipstick shows a trace of leucocytes and no nitrites, and a midstream specimen has been sent. The ultrasound performed an hour ago could not visualise the appendix and reports normal kidneys and normal ovaries.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness in the right abdomen approximately 4 cm above the umbilicus with voluntary guarding and no rebound or rigidity, uterus soft and non-tender with fundal height consistent with dates, no renal angle tenderness, cervical os closed on speculum with no discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (pregnancy range 6.0-16.0), neutrophils 13.1 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), urine dipstick with trace leucocytes and no nitrites, transabdominal ultrasound not visualising the appendix with normal kidneys and normal ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast medium
options.rationale: Computed tomography is accurate but delivers ionising radiation to the foetus and is reserved for situations where magnetic resonance is unavailable or the mother is too unstable to tolerate it. The near pair is that both cross sectional studies answer the question and only one avoids radiation. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

options.text: Repeat transabdominal ultrasound in twelve hours with serial abdominal examination
options.rationale: Serial assessment suits equivocal pain with normal inflammatory markers and no fever, whereas she has a temperature of 38.1 with a C reactive protein of 68 and rising pain. Perforation risk climbs steeply after 24 hours and fetal loss follows perforation in a substantial minority. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with observation and reassessment by the surgical team later
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone are used for a walled off inflammatory mass on imaging, which has not been demonstrated, and starting them without a diagnosis blunts the signs that would otherwise force a decision. The diagnostic question has to be settled first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen performed without gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: When ultrasound fails to visualise the appendix in a pregnant woman with a convincing clinical picture, magnetic resonance imaging is the recommended next study because it images the right iliac fossa reliably without ionising radiation and reduces the negative appendicectomy rate. Gadolinium is avoided because it crosses the placenta. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy on the emergency list without any further imaging beforehand
options.rationale: Proceeding straight to theatre is correct when the picture is unequivocal with peritonism, and she has voluntary guarding without rebound or rigidity alongside an unconfirmed diagnosis. Negative appendicectomy in pregnancy carries a measurable rate of foetal loss and preterm birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Appendicitis is the commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy, affecting roughly one in a thousand pregnancies, and it is harder to recognise because the enlarging uterus displaces the appendix upward and laterally, nausea and vomiting are expected in pregnancy, and the white cell count rises physiologically to as high as 16 x10 to the ninth per litre. Ultrasound is the first imaging study because it is safe and available, but the appendix is not visualised in a large proportion of pregnant women, particularly in the second and third trimesters. Magnetic resonance imaging without gadolinium has become the recommended second line study in Australian practice, with high sensitivity and specificity and no ionising radiation, and it substantially reduces the number of normal appendices removed. Delay is the real danger, since perforation rates rise sharply after 24 hours of symptoms and foetal loss follows perforation far more often than it follows an uncomplicated operation.
key_points: The appendix migrates upward and laterally as the uterus enlarges
A white cell count up to 16 x10^9/L can be physiological in pregnancy
Ultrasound frequently fails to visualise the appendix after the first trimester
Magnetic resonance without gadolinium is the recommended second line study
Perforation rather than surgery is what threatens the pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Gadolinium crosses the placenta and is associated with adverse neonatal outcomes, so magnetic resonance in pregnancy is performed unenhanced, and an unenhanced study is sufficient to diagnose or exclude appendicitis in the great majority of cases.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Appendicitis in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Contraceptive choice for a woman with focal epilepsy on carbamazepine who has already conceived once on a combined pill and does not want pregnancy for five years
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman with focal epilepsy that has been seizure free for three years on carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily. She conceived unexpectedly two years ago while taking a combined oral contraceptive every day and had a termination.

She has two children, does not want another pregnancy for at least five years, and is adamant she will not rely on remembering anything daily. She has heavy but regular periods and a haemoglobin of 112 g/L. Her blood pressure is normal, she does not smoke and she has no history of thrombosis. Her neurologist has documented that carbamazepine is the only agent that has controlled her seizures and wants it continued.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg per square metre, cardiovascular and abdominal examination normal, pelvic examination normal with a mobile anteverted uterus
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155), ferritin 16 micrograms per litre (30-200), urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which contraceptive method should you recommend first?

options.text: A subdermal etonogestrel implant inserted at the next available clinic appointment
options.rationale: The implant is long acting and requires no daily action, but the progestogen it releases is cleared systemically and enzyme inducing drugs lower the circulating level enough to risk failure. The near pair is that both are progestogen devices yet only the intrauterine one escapes hepatic induction. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive containing 50 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol daily
options.rationale: Increasing the oestrogen dose to compensate for induction is not reliable, is unlicensed for this purpose and she has already conceived on a combined pill. It also returns her to the daily regimen she has explicitly rejected. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: A progestogen only pill taken continuously with condoms used as a second method
options.rationale: Oral progestogen is also subject to enzyme induction and depends on daily adherence within a narrow window, and adding condoms shifts the burden of effectiveness onto a method with a high typical use failure rate. Neither element matches a five year plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.text: A three monthly depot medroxyprogesterone injection with a shortened dosing interval
options.rationale: The injection is one of the few systemic progestogen methods that remains effective with enzyme inducing drugs, so the standard interval is retained rather than shortened, but it neither lasts five years nor reduces her menstrual loss. Shortening the interval adds bone exposure for no benefit. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system inserted at the next available appointment
options.rationale: The intrauterine route delivers progestogen locally so hepatic enzyme induction does not reduce its contraceptive effect, and it gives five or more years of cover with no daily action required. It also reduces menstrual loss substantially, which matters with her iron deficiency. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

explanation.summary: Enzyme inducing antiepileptic drugs including carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone, primidone, topiramate at higher doses and oxcarbazepine accelerate hepatic metabolism of systemically absorbed steroid hormones, reducing the effectiveness of the combined pill, the progestogen only pill, the implant and emergency levonorgestrel. The methods that are unaffected are the copper intrauterine device, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, whose action is predominantly local, and the depot injection, which achieves levels high enough to remain reliable at the usual interval. The interaction also runs the other way for some combinations, since oestrogen containing contraception lowers lamotrigine levels and risks seizures. Choosing well matters disproportionately here because unplanned pregnancy on a teratogenic antiepileptic carries a substantial risk of major malformation, and preconception folate and drug review should be discussed at the same visit.
key_points: Enzyme inducers reduce the efficacy of the pill, the mini pill and the implant
Both intrauterine devices and the depot injection remain effective
Raising the oestrogen dose is not a reliable workaround
Oestrogen containing contraception lowers lamotrigine levels
The intrauterine system also treats heavy menstrual loss
explanation.pearls: A woman on an enzyme inducing antiepileptic who needs emergency contraception should be offered a copper intrauterine device, and if she declines, the oral levonorgestrel dose is doubled to 3 mg, because the standard 1.5 mg dose is substantially less effective under induction.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health
